articles.title: In Defense of Abolition
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: At the July DSA National Political Committee (NPC) meeting, I proposed adding abolition to the Workers Deserve More program because I believe that abolishing capitalist policing and prisons is a fundamental demand of the socialist movement. I crafted the language carefully to clarify that we mean abolishing policing and prisons as institutions of capitalist rule, not conflating the abolition of capitalist policing and prisons with the abolition of every future social capacity for accountability and safety. The specific language we added is in italics: “Demilitarize police departments, disempower police unions, and redirect police and prison funding to public services, as steps towards abolishing the carceral forces of the capitalist state. ” This phrasing was eventually simplified to “towards abolishing the police and prison system.” This amendment was opposed by the Socialist Majority and Groundwork caucuses. Soon after the program’s launch, the abolition plank came under criticism from some DSA members , and several endorsed electeds explicitly disavowed the demand. Here, I argue that these reactions are rooted in a misunderstanding of the socialist tradition of abolition, a misreading of the lessons of 2020, and ultimately serve a reformist, anti-revolutionary conclusion. Abolition and Marxism Underlying the current debate over abolition are two recurring misunderstandings. The first, common among liberals and reformists, conflates the abolition of capitalist policing and prisons with the abolition of any future capacity for collective safety, accountability, or restraint. The second, more common in anarchist traditions, rejects the Marxist understanding of the state itself. Marxists reject both errors by analyzing policing and prisons as institutions historically produced by particular class relations, rather than timeless expressions of coercion. Resolving both misunderstandings requires a historical materialist theory of the state and its carceral institutions. A Marxist analysis asks the questions: What social relations produced this institution? What class function does it perform? What material conditions make it necessary? The Liberal Reformist Error Marxism differs from liberalism on the question of the state. Liberalism views the state as an essentially neutral instrument that can be put to different purposes. Marxism instead asks what class relations produced particular state institutions, what functions they serve within those relations, and how they can be transformed and how society’s material conditions can be changed. If, after the revolution, we have socialized the means of production, broken the profoundly corrupting ideological and cultural grip of capitalism, reimagined healthcare, housing, education, social services, and our communities around human need, what will we do with the rare person who remains hellbent on committing violence? How can we provide them with as much care and as many resources as we can while ensuring they are separated from the people they intend to hurt? It is absurd for a Marxist to equate revolutionary institutions of safety, accountability, and care with the institution of policing and prisons under capitalism or to abandon abolition as a rallying call. The possibilities of harm under any social arrangement do not establish the necessity of the institutions through which capitalist society currently manages that arrangement. Our task is to abolish those institutions and transform the social conditions that reproduce violence, not promise that socialism will make every violent act impossible. A related argument for “carceral minimalism” by Loïc Wacquant and, more recently, Paul Heideman in Jacobin , posits that abolition is not a viable path to social justice. Wacquant explicitly understands abolition to entail eliminating the “triad” of police, courts, and prisons rather than merely shrinking or reforming them. He correctly argues that we must take victims’ safety seriously and fight to materially reduce incarceration and state violence under existing conditions, but his framework never escapes a liberal capitalist horizon. He asks how policing, courts, and prisons can be made more limited and humane under capitalism, not whether the social relations that produce and sustain these institutions can be overcome. Indeed, his piece doesn’t mention socialism or communism a single time. The persistence of violence therefore becomes a reason to preserve some version of the institutions through which capitalist society currently manages it. A Marxist abolition rejects this inference and seeks to transform the material conditions that reproduce violence while developing new, democratically controlled capacities for collective safety, accountability, and repair. A socialist society might, where absolutely necessary, separate people who are a danger to others while providing them with care. But Wacquant’s insistence that a penal state, as a specialized apparatus of class domination, is a permanent requirement of complex society mistakes a historically specific institution of class rule for a universal social necessity. His “carceral minimalism” ultimately offers a program for managing coercion from within liberal capitalism, not a socialist alternative to it. The Anarchist Error The liberal error conflates abolition of policing with the abolition of all social accountability; the anarchist error mistakes the Marxist theory of the state for a defense of the capitalist state itself and locates the root of oppression primarily in hierarchy, bureaucracy, and coercion rather than the class relations that give the state and its instruments their political character. Lenin outlines his conception of the state in The State and Revolution . He writes that “the state is a product and a manifestation of the irreconcilability of class antagonisms.” It arises when society becomes divided into antagonistic classes. Here, Lenin quotes Engels, who writes that the state “becomes a power seemingly standing above society,” a “special, public power” that “does not directly coincide” with the people, consisting of “special bodies of armed men,” and “a standing army and police ” as “the chief instruments of state power.” Lenin does not define the state or policing merely as a form of coercion but as the product and a manifestation of the irreconcilability of class antagonisms. The capitalist state is an organ of capitalist rule produced by class society and used by the capitalist class to maintain its domination. The police serve as one of its chief instruments. The proletarian state exists to defend the revolution against capitalist counterrevolution while creating the material conditions for its own obsolescence. As class antagonisms are overcome, coercive institutions produced by class antagonisms lose their social basis. Some critics of abolition correctly identify this need to defend the revolution, but both fail to understand the difference in political character of coercion under socialism and fail to envision a world beyond class antagonism. This is ultimately an anti-communist perspective. Marx’s analysis of the Paris Commune in The Civil War in France makes this distinction concrete. He argues “the working class cannot simply lay hold of the ready-made state machinery, and wield it for its own purposes,” specifically identifying the standing army, police, and bureaucracy. Marx praises the commune because it “got rid” of these institutions and transferred their functions to serve the working class, rather than simply inheriting them: “Instead of continuing to be the agent of the Central Government, the police was at once stripped of its political attributes, and turned into the responsible, and at all times revocable, agent of the Commune … having once got rid of the standing army and the police —the physical force elements of the old government.” He continues: “Wonderful, indeed, was the change the Commune had wrought in Paris! No more corpses at the morgue, no nocturnal burglaries, scarcely any robberies; in fact, for the first time since the days of February 1848, the streets of Paris were safe, and that without any police of any kind.” This is the materialist basis for a socialist abolitionism. We seek the abolition of prisons and policing as institutions of capitalist domination, while recognizing that socialism will have to solve real problems that capitalism currently purports to address through those institutions. The Marxist question is not whether those problems exist nor whether society may ever require coercive measures, but what social relations make particular forms of coercion necessary, who controls them, what class interests they serve, and how the institutions reproduce the conditions that make them necessary. In this way, abolition is not a demand to abolish social protection or accountability but a demand to abolish the capitalist form through which these problems are organized, and to transform the underlying social conditions so that institutions of class domination are unnecessary. The Rise of Abolition Tracing the roots of abolition reveals its significance to the socialist movement. During the George Floyd uprisings in 2020, abolition was a central concern in socialist politics. At its strongest, the movement came to understand abolition as not only a moral appeal against punishment in the abstract but a fight against police and prisons as institutions rooted in the history of slavery, racial capitalism, and class rule, whose abolition required transforming the social conditions that reproduce them. This framing is rooted in the Black radical socialist tradition. From W.E.B. Du Bois to Angela Davis and Ruth Wilson Gilmore, abolition has long meant abolition of the social order that makes systems of policing and prisons necessary while constructing new capacities for collective life. Du Bois located the origins of modern policing and imprisonment in the unfinished project of abolishing slavery. As he wrote in Black Reconstruction , “The slave went free; stood a brief moment in the sun; then moved back again toward slavery.” The overthrow of chattel slavery was followed by new forms of racial domination, including convict leasing, Jim Crow, debt peonage, and modern policing, extending slavery’s social function under capitalism by ensuring a disciplined and racially stratified labor force produced by Black oppression. Gilmore extends this analysis to the political economy of prisons in the neoliberal era. The disruption and disorganization of the working class is essential to the functioning of the system. As she writes in Abolition Geography, “Put simply, capitalism requires inequality and racism enshrines it. Thus criminalization and mass incarceration are class war.” In Golden Gulag , Gilmore analyzes how the carceral system became a means of managing the crises produced by neoliberal capitalism . The economic crises arising from the neoliberal transformation of the capitalist economy produced a massive increase in surplus labor — a growing population of people whose labor was considered superfluous to capital’s needs. Because of the racialized hierarchy of social relations in the United States, one key response was a massively intensified campaign to criminalize Black and Latino populations, and a concomitant enormous growth of the carceral state. This transformed a surplus population into one to be managed and contained, which weakened the possibility of the solidarity required to meaningfully challenge capitalism. As Gilmore explains, “Capital must be able to get rid of workers whose labor power is no longer desirable — whether permanently, by mechanical or human replacement, or temporarily by layoffs — and have access to new or previously idled labor as the need arises. These necessities, as Marx’s science of capital accumulation demonstrates, are not due to the personalities or preferences of heads of firms: CEOs who resist such “adjustments” to the labor force jeopardize profits.” Today we see the hyper-criminalization of immigrants as serving a similarly useful role for capitalism. U.S. imperialism creates the conditions for mass migration through practices of unequal exchange that impoverish the Global South, where the resulting sub-subsistence level wages force workers to migrate for survival. The creation of a maximally exploitable immigrant labor produces an underclass of laborers whose vulnerability is targeted to drive down the power of the working class as a whole. (See Migration As Economic Imperialism by Immanuel Ness.) Declining opportunities for profitable investment for capital dictate that workers in the United States must be disciplined to accept less, and a terrified, hyper-exploitable working class continues to lower the floor for the working class as a whole. As Mark Neocleous summarizes in A Critical Theory of Police Power, “Capital is nothing less than a social war and the conflict between classes the most significant civil war in history. Yet this class war is carried out as a generalized police war.” Given the centrality of policing and prisons to capitalist accumulation within the imperial core, abandoning abolition would mean abandoning class war. Abolition’s Retreat Today there is a growing retreat from the Marxist and Black radical frameworks. Much of the current debate frames abolition as an abstract hypothetical about whether any society will ever require coercion or restraint. This framing detaches itself from the concrete institutions and social relations through which policing is organized under capitalism. Instead of asking what police and prisons are as institutions that manage the contradictions of racial capitalism, it asks whether a generalized form of public safety might exist in an imagined future society. In contrast, a Marxist approach asks us to begin not with abstractions but with the concrete institutions and social relations that produce institutions. Police and prisons are not neutral responses to human conflict but historically specific institutions expanded alongside capitalism, colonialism, and racial domination. The consequences of this mistake are significant. Once abolition is framed as an abstract proposition that all coercion must vanish forever, it becomes easy to dismiss as unrealistic. Instead of being seen as a strategy for dismantling institutions that reproduce capitalism and racial domination, it’s framed as either the fantastical idealism of anarchism or the limited purview of policy reform. It’s important to acknowledge that this retreat from abolition emerges from a real contradiction facing the socialist movement. The George Floyd uprising was the largest mass rebellion against policing in a generation, yet it produced few lasting structural victories. It’s reasonable to ask whether the movement’s politics, including the rallying cry to abolish the police, contributed to that outcome. But this mistakes the primary lessons of 2020. The principal failure was not that abolition proved to be bad politics or messaging, but that the socialist movement lacked the durable organization, institutions, mass base, and independent politics necessary to adequately absorb the energy of the uprising and carry it forward once the streets emptied. This retreat also cannot be understood apart from the intensity of the capitalist and political backlash against the politics of 2020. As Alex Karakatsanis has shown , the liberal establishment and corporate media worked overtime to co-opt the outrage into reforms that left the core institutions intact and quickly began a massive propaganda campaign aimed at selling the lie that crime was spiraling out of control. Progressive politicians and liberal media were eager to return to business as usual, abandoning the rhetoric of 2020 as quickly as they could and once again supporting ballooning police budgets, happy to paper over their inability to meet people’s needs by throwing money at the criminalization of poverty in service of capital. At the same time, much of the left increasingly reduced policing to a question of municipal budgets rather than understanding it as a central institution of capitalist political power. The basis of this liberal retreat from abolition is clear. The question remaining is: What are the core contradictions driving the left’s retreat? Electoralism and Reformism DSA’s electoral successes have been expanding at a rapid rate. As a result, anything that appears to threaten this success naturally faces special scrutiny. This reformist logic was recently articulated by Mayor Mamdani , who, when asked about his breaks with DSA, stated: “Especially when it comes to public safety, I’ve been very clear that we have our police force, we have prisons, we have jails. The purpose of these is also to ensure we are delivering safety & justice.” Indeed, members of the Socialist Majority Caucus and Groundwork caucuses, the Jacobin editorial board, and a number of DSA electeds and aligned candidates have argued that abolition should be de-emphasized or abandoned because it is electorally unpopular or idealistic. Often, this takes the form of stressing the urgency of passing a candidate’s affordability agenda at all costs. This risks pushing DSA towards the pitfalls of tailism and economism , subverting our political program in favor of what is immediately achievable rather than using our political organization to expand what workers see as possible. It is of course necessary to adapt the way we communicate depending on the context. Every mass movement must distinguish between propaganda, agitation, and the demands most appropriate to a particular audience. The error lies in retreating from a political plank altogether to avoid the strategic challenge in the first place. Whether a particular candidate campaigns on abolition, and to what extent, is a tactical question. But allowing that question to redefine the political program of a socialist movement reverses the proper relationship between the movement and its elected officials. Independent socialist organizations must expand the political horizon of the working class, not narrow it according to what elected officials can comfortably defend. DSA’s success is because of our steadfast adherence to our core principles, not in spite of it. Our organization has grown significantly since our program was released. When another moment like 2020 occurs (and it is inevitable), the working class will remember where we stood. Part of this challenge reflects the need for DSA to develop further towards a party of the working class: an organization with all the structure, resources, political coherence, and discipline to support our candidates in standing firm rather than leaving them isolated in their respective political arenas to fend off attacks and feel compelled to distance themselves from or abandon demands in order to win reelection or fulfill campaign promises. That requires a commitment to fulfilling our Convention mandate to build DSA’s capacity to act as an independent political organization: strengthening the National Electoral Commission’s ability to coordinate our electoral work nationally while building robust Socialists in Office programs at the local level, so our electeds remain closely connected to DSA and are not left to navigate the pressures of office alone. It also requires building connective tissue and infrastructure across chapters and between national and local levels so that DSA can act as a unified political organization rather than a collection of isolated electoral campaigns. Of course, embracing an abolitionist horizon does not mean DSA and our electeds should abstain from reform. Socialists in office should pursue every reform that weakens the carceral state, defunds police, reduces incarceration, and expands healthcare, but they should do so as part of a strategy aimed at the eventual abolition of policing and prisons rather than as an end in itself. For Marxists, abolition is not an abstract moral principle or a distant utopia. It’s the unfinished struggle to complete the destruction of slavery’s institutional legacy and embrace Marx’s call to seize the machinery of the state, smash it altogether, and usher in a new social order. We should recall Eugene Debs’s exhortation: While there is a soul in prison, we are not free. articles.title: Americans Are Turning Against School Vouchers
articles.author: Jennifer C. Berkshire
articles.content: Ten percent. That’s how many Arizonans support that state’s Wild West voucher scheme. If the figure seems surprising given the ardency of the sales pitch for “education freedom,” its source should send your eyebrows skyward. This bleak view of Arizona public opinion about the state’s $1-billion-plus Education Savings Account (ESA) program comes not from voucher haters but from their superfans: the American Federation for Children (AFC), the deep-pocketed and highly influential school-choice lobbying firm started by Betsy DeVos. To understand why AFC is decidedly downcast even as vouchers are on the move, we need to make a trip to the Grand Canyon State, where last month, the state Supreme Court deprived voters of the opportunity to weigh in on whether the famously fraud-ridden voucher program should be more tightly regulated. The backstory is complicated — riddled with backstabbing, late-night shenanigans , and dueling ballot questions — which is why we’re speeding ahead to the aftermath. While Arizona’s pro-voucher forces popped the champagne corks over the death of the ESA reform effort, DeVos’s crew sounded a far more cautionary note to the effect of: “This program is deeply unpopular, and unless we crack down on fraud and implement some standards to convince the public that it’s actually working, vouchers in Arizona are doomed.” Not Just an Arizona Problem As a tireless, albeit increasingly weary chronicler of the intersection of politics and education, signs of a split within the school-choice coalition are my equivalent of catnip. It also confirms the argument that I’ve been making that the politics of “education freedom” are not just unsustainable but hurting the GOP at the polls. Here’s the short version. While the idea of school choice may be very popular in the abstract, the universal programs that red state legislatures have rammed through in recent years deeply rankle voters. Talk to virtually any Democrat running, or winning, in a state with one of these programs on the books, and they’ll tell you that support for reforming and scaling back vouchers is nearly universal. Here’s Emily Gregory, a Democratic legislator in Florida, where vouchers are spreading like a red algae bloom, on what she’s been hearing from her constituents:“I hear unity,” she says. “I hear bipartisan support in the community — that these are reasonable expectations of accountability for taxpayer dollars.” Gregory flipped a seat in the Florida legislature last spring, besting her GOP opponent via a campaign that stressed affordability and support for public education — and now represents the Palm Beach district that includes Mar-a-Lago. Meet the School-Choice Extremists So if voucher reform really is a unifying cause, as suggested by a growing list of red-to-blue flips and the dire warnings of none other than Betsy DeVos’s lobby shop, why do red state legislators seem to be moving in the opposite direction? Here is where we introduce a new character to our education freedom tapestry. Let’s call him the “school-choice extremist,” an increasingly prominent figure in states where unregulated voucher programs are busting budgets and sowing political consternation. Take West Virginia, for example, where, back in 2021, supermajority GOP state legislatures enthusiastically enacted what’s been called the nation’s “broadest” voucher program. Fast-forward a few years, and that program is draining the state’s coffers and enabling a school closure crisis . Alas, GOP lawmakers like the chair of the House Finance Committee who called for “modest guardrails” for the program are no longer in office, having been primaried, thanks to a sea of out-of-state school-choice money and the governor, who wants unlimited funding for vouchers. As for the cause of school-choice extremism, chalk it up to too much time spent in an echo chamber, which leads prominent pro-voucher voices like Jason Huffman and Jason Bedrick to become convinced that any criticism of voucher programs is either a leftist plot and/or the work of a single investigative reporter. A Flawed Theory of Change To make sense of the emerging conflict within the voucher coalition, we have to revisit the case for making vouchers universal as articulated by the school-choice evangelist formerly known as Seth Rose . In his 2024 book, The Parent Revolution , Corey DeAngelis laid out the case for 1) abandoning the civil rights justification for school choice in favor of 2) leaning into/pouring fuel on the school culture wars and 3) making even the wealthiest parents eligible to have their private school tuition paid for by the public. As DeAngelis explained, while more targeted programs were vulnerable to the changing political tides, as in the GOP’s decision to roll back civil rights, empowering the most affluent parents would create a built-in lobby group that politicians would find hard to buck. But while DeAngelis may have been correct about the political heft of wealthy voucher users, he seems to have forgotten about another key group: the public. DeAngelis, you might recall, was formerly in the employ of the American Federation for Children, which cut ties with him after his previous career as a porn star came to light. Which makes it all the more interesting that AFC is now sounding the alarm regarding the lack of public support for vouchers. AFC Senior Fellow Patrick Graff, for instance, warned that the GOP’s insistence on a “black box” approach to school choice is unsustainable. Public policies have multiple constituencies and, in addition to the students using the program, another is the general public — a group whose opinion is especially important if you want to maintain the program. Failing to provide any information on how students in the program are performing academically is putting the school-choice movement increasingly out of step with what voters expect of education programs, especially one that costs over $1 billion every year. Meet the Flippers The only poll that ultimately matters, the one on Election Day, keeps showing us that public anger over waste, fraud, and abuse in voucher programs has become a potent source of support for Democrats. In Arizona, where Democrats have a realistic shot at flipping the state legislature, candidates have been focusing relentlessly on the need to reform the voucher program, because they know it’s an issue that voters care about. While advocates may have fallen short of the support they needed to put the Protect Education Act on the ballot this fall, they still managed to collect some 420,000 signatures in fourteen weeks, engaging in roughly one million conversations in the process. That’s precisely the political vulnerability that’s got the AFC so worried, and justifiably so. The bigger and more expensive these programs get, the more pressure there will be to reform them, even as GOP-dominated legislatures remain under the thrall of school-choice extremists. (There’s an irony here, which is that AFC created this dilemma by primarying even mild school-choice skeptics, often replacing them with more fringe extremists.) But for now, I see no evidence that the GOP understands how toxic this issue is becoming. In Texas, for example, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is running neck and neck with incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, voucher proponents now want the legislature to double the size of the controversial new program, even as many conservatives in the state remain furious over its existence. The good news is that at least some Democrats finally seem to be realizing that anger over unchecked voucher programs crosses lines of party, class, and geography, especially as public schools are drained of resources or close altogether. The bad news? Not all Democrats, as they say. That may be the greatest irony of all. Even as the wave of anti-voucher sentiment helps the party flip statehouses and claim governors’ mansions, the Democrat-led campaign to get blue state governors to opt in to Donald Trump’s federal voucher program is only intensifying.

articles.title: Economics Needs a New Approach to Inflation
articles.author: Andrew Elrod
articles.content: Four years have passed since the COVID-19 pandemic’s inflation in the wake of the American economy’s reopening hit its peak, and the American business cycle is today in a strange way. Wanting to slow the rise in prices that accompanied the reopening and construction boom, the Biden administration and the Federal Reserve cut social spending and raised interest rates. Nonresidential construction has been falling since late 2023. Residential construction investment collapsed in early 2023, then rose briefly in 2024, but has been falling for over a year now. As the unemployment rate crept up slowly throughout the second half of the Biden administration, economists and journalists consistently warned of the risk of a recession. Yet despite falling construction spending and creeping unemployment, the recession never came. Instead, nearly two years into a change in management, the American economy in the summer of 2026 was again seeing accelerating inflation. Having fallen from 9 to 3 percent during the Biden administration and stabilizing below that through the presidential election and the chaos of the new tariffs of “Liberation Day,” the annual rate of the change of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the monthly report most commonly used to measure inflation, rose from 2.4 percent in February to 4.2 percent in May. Driven by petroleum products — motor fuel, fuel oil, and natural gas, primarily — the course of prices has closely followed the Iran war: slowing considerably with news of the sixty-day Memorandum of Understanding in June and July. The August inflation report, released September 11, maintains this brisker pace of 3.4 percent. With all eyes in finance waiting to see what action the Federal Reserve takes in response, the news reinforces expectations for an increase in short-term interest rates at its policy meeting next week. Data center construction has been propping up the construction industry, and that has rested on a credit boom that may become more difficult to roll over if interest rates increase further. While the stock market continues to boom, as last year’s top-end and corporate tax cuts leave more money for the wealthy to invest speculatively, median wage growth has fallen so far that even the 3.4 and 3.3 percent inflation of recent months means workers’ income is falling in real terms. “The biggest worry,” explains the Wall Street Journal , “is that current, elevated inflation levels could work their way into people’s inflation expectations — which can in turn affect future inflation.” This is because, according to the conventional wisdom, higher prices threaten higher wages. “If workers believe inflation will remain high,” the Journal continues, “they can push for wage increases beyond the price increases they have already seen.” If the Federal Reserve raises interest rates next week, the official justification will be to stop such a wage-price spiral from turning. Why has the Federal Reserve become the institution to which presidents, Congress, businessmen, and journalists instinctively turn when considering what to do about inflation? Last year, two economists offered a rather startling answer. As Mark Blyth and Nicolò Fraccaroli explain in Inflation: A Guide for Users and Losers , the academic economics profession has since the 1970s constructed a self-congratulatory delusion about the role of central bank inflation targeting and central bank independence. “[O]ur underlying theories of inflation are quite fragile,” they explain, resting less on rigorous science than on partisan humanities — namely, history. And it is precisely to mask this fragile intellectual foundation on which “the field as a whole not only agrees . . . but upon which it bases many of its core concepts and hence its authority claims” that the intellectual politics of inflation have become so closed with its return since the coronavirus pandemic. Good, Bad, and Ugly Inflation While these conclusions may not come as a surprise to those who came of age during the Great Recession, the publication last year of this short, earnest, and plaintive but restrained book is worth considering not only for its argument but for the identity of its authors. Fraccaroli is an economist at the World Bank, one of the two international financial organizations, along with the International Monetary Fund, created after World War II to govern international finance and development. He is also a visiting professor at Brown, where Blyth is a professor of international economics. The authors have their feet in the worlds of mainstream academic macro-finance, understand that economics is the “language of power” that “sets the field of play for everyone else,” and are therefore concerned that “the ideas of the 1970s and the institutions that they spawned in the ’80s that were supposed to safeguard us against inflation” — independent central banks with inflation targets — “nstead made us more vulnerable to its return.” In making this argument, they have to cover a lot of ground, and the speed with which they do so may diminish the force of what they are saying. What should land with the impact of a meteorite is obscured by the orbit required to survey the landscape of “mainstream” consensus on inflation and inflation policy: what is measured and how; how economists theorize and conjecture about the relationship among measured variables; how central the unmeasurable variables have become to the consensus; and how governments and business typically interpret and react to those measurements. About half the book is made up of this background material. To establish that there are “different kinds of inflation,” Blyth and Fraccaroli employ the spaghetti western terminology of Fabio Panetta, the governor of the Bank of Italy: “the good, the bad, and the ugly.” “Good” inflation is where “wages, in theory at least, rise in line with workers’ productivity” — around 2 percent, though some have advocated for 3 — and “even if prices increase, wages are catching up, and people can afford the same amount of goods, if not more.” “Bad” inflation is a onetime jump in prices, kicked off usually by some single-industry or country problem: Ukrainian wheat and Russian oil getting cut off in 2022, for example, before Brazilian and Persian Gulf supplies could meet the higher price level. “Ugly” inflation is when “prices and wages push each other upward in a cycle,” and the “bad” inflation kicks into a self-sustaining race between companies, workers, households, and investors to stay ahead of the game. Such distinctions are tolerated within the mainstream. Nobody disputed that there were different kinds of inflation in Washington in 2021: the debate within the mainstream was whether the bad inflation that began that year would turn ugly without austerity and interest rate hikes — whether it was “transitory.” What economists disagree about is how a bad inflation turns ugly. Arguing the point requires what Blyth and Fraccaroli call “inflation storytelling,” the narratives constructed to explain causal relationships in the price system. For “team transitory,” during the pandemic inflation, the story was that the price level rise was a one-off event. “Let markets work” was a common refrain of progressive economists opposed to Federal Reserve interest rate increases in late 2021: having jumped from 1.3 to 6.2 percent in the first ten months of 2021, the inflation would slow and come down as supply caught up to demand on its own. In the terms of economic theory, inflation “expectations” remained “anchored.” “Team permanent,” their intellectual opponents both within the White House and among its partisan enemies, told different stories: excessive government spending from the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act and the American Rescue Plan was raising household spending or creating a disincentive to work, reducing supply; too-tight labor markets from lockdowns, or lazy or greedy workers, were pushing wages up too far, too fast. In economic theory terms, “expectations” were becoming “de-anchored.” The ease with which national broadcast media slipped into the “labor shortage” hysteria of late 2021 and 2022, as the inflation accelerated, demonstrated the stakes of these narratives. The failure of the 2021–22 Congress to pass a budget for the administration’s first full fiscal year until ten months after it began demonstrated their effectiveness. Missing from this account of the Joe Biden years is what most people actually believed. Blyth and Fraccaroli cite a May 2022 survey from Deloitte that found 60 percent of Americans thought “companies are taking advantage” of the pandemic “by raising prices beyond their own rising operating costs in an attempt to increase profit.” While economists and journalists disagreed among themselves about whether or when the Federal Reserve should raise rates, they agreed almost unanimously that this was wrong. Blyth and Fraccaroli rely heavily on the example of Isabella Weber , the professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, who argued in late 2021 that the reason the inflation had not subsided was the expansion of corporate profits, particularly in monopolistic industries. Controversy ensued. The existence of the Deloitte survey is itself an artifact of how profoundly challenging the perspective was to what those who control major corporations were willing to countenance: six months after the Guardian published Weber’s infamous opinion, the world’s largest accounting firm, itself a key multinational corporation organizing the informational lifeblood of capitalism, felt compelled to test the popularity of the idea. They found that what a majority of people believed squared with Weber’s contention. Even though this is the story “that intuitively most people think is right,” Blyth and Fraccaroli note how “economists hate it with a strange passion.” The reason for that is not obvious from the perspective of economic theory. While orthodox price theory holds that in a competitive market, a ceiling on price will prevent the expansion of supply, resulting in shortages, nearly a century of research on “imperfect competition” and “oligopoly” has demonstrated what anyone in America knows about corporate competition: most industries have a few key players that drive what the industry as a whole is doing. Whether like oil refining, in which “[o]ne firm leads the price increase, and the others follow,” or the much more common “market structure of oligopoly, in which a handful of firms can set prices above marginal cost, but only if they cooperate with each other,” pricing arrangements in which sellers have a degree of discretion over profit margins exist across the range of real-world market structures. The relevance of this fact for theories of inflation is not that corporate pricing power can kick off inflation. Usually, the risk of losing market share prevents this. Rather, the existence of “imperfect” or “monopolistic” competition means that when a bad inflation does occur, owing to a natural disaster or war or other “supply shock,” it can become a pretext for the kinds of collective action among corporations that would not normally be possible. The resulting price rise in some parts of the economy becomes rising costs for others, and it is in that moment that businesses can act together to raise the general level of prices. As Blyth and Fraccaroli explain the logic resuscitated in the work of Weber and her colleague Evan Wasner, “price gouging may not be the fundamental cause of inflation, but once inflation gets going it’s arguably a large part of what keeps it going.” Demonstrating the relevance of the point to inflation theory, they cite one survey of retail corporation earnings calls from late 2021 as finding that 56 percent of companies admitted to shareholders “that inflation gave them the ability to raise prices far beyond what they would have needed to offset higher production costs.” If you think profits play a role in inflation, Blyth and Fraccaroli write, then the reason “inflation is higher in the United States than in Europe [is] simply because the American economy is more concentrated, and a handful of firms in critical sectors can set prices because they don’t face significant competition and the government does not enforce antitrust laws.” The reason this occurs is because “those firms are critical funders of those hugely expensive US elections that elect the folks who regulate these firms.” Diagnosing the nexus of government and business power as the cause of inflation is not likely to be popular among those who hold power, and those who speak on their behalf have adjusted accordingly. The Macroeconomic Consensus on Inflation Is Wrong Arguing for the profit-push theory of the covid inflation, however, is not the primary purpose of Inflation: A Guide for Losers and Users . As the self-effacing title hints, the goal is to understand why, even though the evidence for it is “actually quite plentiful,” the profit-push theory of inflation “is always contested by mainstream economists.” The taboo rests on where “storytelling” departs from social science. All four of the types of inflation stories they catalog — excess demand, excessive wage increases, supply shocks, and corporate profits — draw from different combinations of scientific work. But only one of these stories, the story of corporate profits, is met by mainstream economics as a challenge to “both the field and its members’ claim to authority.” This is because the corporate profits story challenges the theory at the basis of the academic consensus. The “transitory” debate in Washington ultimately turned on the theory of “anchored expectations,” the idea that workers would not continue to demand double-digit wage increases, and companies would stop raising prices, because all knew the inflation would ultimately end. For “team permanent,” stories about excess demand,” a change in the “Phillips curve” (the relationship of inflation and unemployment), or even “the money supply” likewise rested on the theory of “de-anchored expectations,” the idea that the wage-price spiral would continue to turn, because nobody believed it would stop. The disagreement was not about how inflation worked but whether or not “expectations” were becoming “de-anchored.” It is the theory of expectations that economists ultimately rely on to make the case that central banks can control the level of inflation. Indeed, the experience of the pandemic disproved every other mainstream inflation theory. While the historical record shows that central banks raising interest rates has coincided with the end of inflationary business cycle booms, that experience and almost every theory purporting to explain it all rest on higher interest rates causing a recession. But despite aggressive rate increases in 2022 and 2023, the US economy boomed, employment increased rather than decreased, while inflation in the United States came down from 8 percent to 3 percent. “To the extent there is a debate in the mainstream,” Blyth and Fraccoli write, “the question is not really about whether the medicine works but how high the dosage should be.” The recessionless disinflation should be understood as a profound challenge to this assumption of economic policy. It is “disconfirming information” that should force scientific minds to “accept that there is something wrong with the underlying theory.” Instead, the “mainstream response” has been to “praise the Fed.” Why? While the authority of macroeconomics has traditionally rested, like most sciences, on its predictive powers, Blyth and Fraccaroli note how economics has largely surrendered its warrant for prediction since “the failure to foresee the 2008 financial crisis” and the “support for austerity policies after the financial crisis” that resulted in the Great Recession. They also note how “circular” any theory of expectations is: those expectations can only be known by whether inflation is rising or falling. Where does the authority of an increasingly closed and demonstrably unpopular macroeconomic consensus come from, then? Blyth and Fraccaroli come to the conclusion that it no longer rests on scientific claims at all, but rather an interpretation of history. In the United States, that interpretation centers on the Vietnam War, the Arab-Israeli war of 1973, and the Iranian Revolution — what economists, following lay readers, lump together as “the 1970s.” “All academic fields rest upon official histories that tell them how they got to where they are today and why they think the way they do,” they write. The official history of academic macroeconomics is that an excess demand from the Vietnam War and the Great Society brought unemployment too low, empowering workers to demand too much, with inflation spiraling out of control just when the Nixon administration took the leap so controversial to conservative economists of imposing wage and price controls. In the theoretical language of the field, the inflation of the 1970s persisted because “inflation expectations became de-anchored,” meaning that between 1965 and 1982, the price level in the United States tripled because the American public began to expect it to. The inflation ended with the restructuring Volcker Shock and Reagan recession, because with widespread suffering, the American public stopped expecting prices to rise. It is this interpretation of history that economists cite as their bulwark evidence for the theory of expectations that guides inflation policy today. In a remarkably refreshing survey of the politics of the Nixon administration, Blyth and Fraccaroli challenge the official history of the 1970s inflation. “[W]hen we look closely at Nixon’s price controls,” they write, “it is really difficult to conclusively call them a failure.” After all, the controls were mandatory only through the 1972 election, after which the opening act of Richard Nixon’s second term was to declare a “Phase III” of the program in which they became voluntary. Given the opportunity “to make up for all the profits and wages they had forgone in the two prior years,” corporations “hiked prices well beyond the guideposts” in 1973. This was ten months before the Arab oil embargo accelerated the inflation further. “But the damage was done, as was the credibility of price controls as a tool to fight inflation.” While historians of the United States have known this, few have felt the ability to draw judgements from it to challenge conventional economic theory. Not so Blyth and Fraccaroli: “With hindsight, one could argue that the mistake Nixon made was to declare victory too early.” The implications of this interpretation are profound for macroeconomics. “We use interest rates to regulate the economy,” Blyth and Fraccaroli explain, “not because they are the ideal controls, but because in the 1980s we gave up on regulating the level of prices through fiscal means such as price controls, credit limits, and other such devices.” That resignation was driven by a “single-minded fixation on the inflation of the 1970s as being caused by the de-anchoring of agents’ expectations,” with the result that “the institutions we built in the 1980s and ’90s to control inflation,” namely “independent central banks with inflation targets,” were designed with only one theory in mind. Having decided on a solution, the mainstream of the economics profession worked backward toward a theory — the theory of expectations. “Once one understanding of a problem becomes dominant,” Blyth and Fraccaroli write, “the policy apparatus designed to respond to it can respond only in that same way.” The Anti-Inflation Playbook Is Wrong If the “premises” of economic policy “are wrong,” Blyth and Fraccaroli note, “then not only can inflation happen, but the standard policy playbook for fighting inflation will not work. Indeed, it will actively do harm, at least to the many.” Inflation has returned. What will the government, the economics profession that advises them, and the media that draws on economists’ arguments do? Blyth and Fraccaroli’s mission in this context, however noble, appears quixotic. Why would an economics profession entranced by the delusive force of the “disinflationary magic” of expectations consider their challenge? As they note, more than reducing inflation, the point of raising interest rates during an inflation is to protect the wealthy whose income from securities can always rise with bond yields. This fact alone challenges the very concept of central bank independence, as they note, citing research from the Peterson Institute’s Adam Posen that whether an ostensibly independent central bank actually raises interest rates depends more on whether or not that country’s banking system is profiting from inflation. During the era of US wars in Korea and Vietnam, American economists likewise distinguished between kinds of inflation. Rather than “good,” “bad,” or “ugly,” they described inflation in an equestrian metaphor: it was “creeping,” “trotting,” or “galloping.” There was no question then whether a creeping inflation was, just like its faster varieties, also caused by a wage-price spiral. The important difference mid-century economists saw was not between theoretical causes but how fast the spiral was turning. The key to slowing a galloping inflation into a “trot,” as a generation of economists formed in the era of government profit studies and nationwide union wage-setting learned, was to find players to the game capable of exercising restraint and persuading them into doing so — or using the government to compel them. Unlike the theory of expectations, the explanation behind this story is one of power. A bad inflation turns ugly when organized parts of the economy try to raise their income over their costs. The reason the pandemic inflation stabilized was not because the Federal Reserve raised interest rates and “anchored” workers’ expectations, but rather because US workers are not organized in a way that would allow them to keep raising wages. We are unaccustomed to seeing the inflationary process as an economic struggle requiring a conscious truce, whether negotiated or imposed, because so many of us are no longer players to the game. In some sense, the economics profession as a whole has missed the moment. While so much vitriolic ink was spilled in 2021 and 2022 over whether it was appropriate for the president of the United States to acknowledge the role of corporate profits in driving the rising prices of that expansion, today the president simply says consumers are being “gouged” by “the big Oil Companies.” Already, in June, the president instructed the Department of Justice to investigate profiteering among oil refiners, whose margins have grown from between $15 and $20 for each barrel of oil in February to between $67 and $73 today — a 400 to 450 percent increase. (During the Biden inflation, refinery margins peaked around $55–$60 for only three months, less than half the time they’ve been elevated this year.) On September 1, he met with executives from Chevron, Valero, Marathon, and other refinery owners to discuss how to stabilize the price of gasoline and diesel. The right to set prices, what Blyth and Fraccaroli call the “most central of capitalist freedoms,” is already being challenged by the national executive installed by the nation’s leading capitalists. At the same time, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has turned to new tools attempting to blunt one effect of inflation, falling bond prices, as investors anticipate a Federal Reserve interest rate increase. Whether or not these attempts at voluntary jawboning will work is one question. The White House’s desire for cheap gasoline certainly comes into conflict with its opposition to raising corporate taxes. But these are political, rather than economic, problems. In the political system, the causes of inflation are no longer in dispute — except insofar as banks and corporations, and especially media corporations, have economists they can use to argue otherwise. The only relevant question is what power can be organized to do anything about it.

articles.title: Stories from the Chilean Coup: Part 1
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content: By Bridget T First published on Substack here . 9-11-2025 was the 52 nd anniversary of the Chilean coup. Twelve years before that, on the 40th anniversary, 9-11-2013, I walked into a room at the top of Anabel Taylor Hall on the Cornell University campus to take part in an interview that would alter my view of the world forever. Presidential Palace, Chile 1973 In the summer of 2013, I was a Politics student at Ithaca College ready to start an internship with CUSLAR (Committee on U.S. – Latin American Relations) in the fall. I volunteered first for the summer to help organize the CUSLAR Spanish Camp for Activists where we improved our Spanish and empowered each other with good food, music, and political speakers. It was there that I heard live Chilean music for the first time around the campfire. I would later find out it was played by a man named Carlos. This is the same Carlos that I would interview about his experience in leaving Chile after the coup and coming to the U.S. in exile some months later. Political refugees from Chile had come to Ithaca, New York since 1974. My work with CUSLAR that summer also involved researching the connections and ties between Ithaca based organizations, such as CUSLAR and the Friends of Chile, and the larger refugee community that had formed a network to get exiled and imprisoned people out of Chile. From this research, we decided to put together an oral history project in preparation for the 40 th anniversary of the coup. I had the opportunity to hear the stories of those who were in Chile on the day of the coup and the years of President Allende and Unidad Popular’s administration. Each story, or “testimonio,” gives a new perspective on the day itself, and on the years leading up to such a monumental event. Each person’s story represents a new layer of the coup and what it means in world history and in the history of the U.S. empire. Everyone I have ever talked to from Chile had an entirely different experience when their world came to a screeching halt on 9-11-73. I think this speaks to the human condition of course, but also, the truly diverse coalition that had been built around Allende and the thousands of workers who supported him. One story unlike that of anyone else is the testimony from Ana Villa. Ana’s late father was an American diplomat working with the United Nations in Santiago at the time of the coup. Ana’s family was completely uprooted by the events of the 1973 coup. Ana had a unique viewpoint as a young person in Santiago, mingling with the international elite, but also coming of age with the people of Chile before and during the Allende government. I met Ana on 9-11-2013 when she walked into the CUSLAR office accompanied by her mother Fran Barraclough. This is what she said: Experiencing 9-11-73, Santiago, Chile “I’m Annie. Ana Maria. I was born in Tennessee, but grew up mostly in Santiago, Chile. My dad, Solon Barraclough, worked with the United Nations with the FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization), but he also had connections at *ICIRA (The Institute for Land Reform in Chile). So we went to Chile in 1959 and he went down to work for the FAO. I went to Nido de Aguilas and Santiago College which are both international bilingual schools. I was very political, and I disliked all of the rich kids I went to school with. The kids were pretty snobbish. I started becoming very political in 1970 after Allende won the presidential election, and I was a senior at Nido de Aguilas. If the coup hadn’t happened, I never would have graduated because I was never at school! I would go to school and then run away to go to the big marches, in the middle of tear gas and everything. From 1970 onward, every time there was a Unidad Popular march I was there. . . A lot of interesting things happened at the time because of my school being children of ambassadors and international people. “They knew that the coup was supposed to be that Monday” The week of the coup, I went to school on Monday, September 10th and none of the other Americans were there. I asked why there were all gone, and the teacher said they all took a vacation. They all went out on vacation at the same time! That was ridiculous. They knew that the coup was supposed to be that Monday. And they took off. So I thought something was funny that Monday and then on Tuesday, I did not go to school. On September 11th, I was supposed to go to some offices downtown to turn in papers right by La Moneda and I overslept. I overslept that morning. Now I have to explain where our house was. It was up this long street on a hill. A larger house with more land. Right across from us was the military country club. On the day of the coup d’etat, the military ran all of their messages up to the county club all day. Through the months before the coup there was a lot of abnormal activity and many more cars. On the day of the coup, my father happened to be in Israel and my mother was at a friend’s house. I remember waking up in a panic because I’d overslept. I called my neighbor to say “we’ve got to go” and she said “we’re not going anywhere.” “My friend said, ‘No, this is real”’ In June there had been a similar thing. The military had sent tanks up to La Moneda, attempting to do a coup or to scare people. This was called the Tanquetazo, so I said “ah it’s just another Tanquetazo. These sons of bitches don’t know what they’re doing.” But my friend said, “No, this is real.” I got to hear Allende’s speech on the radio. I could look out and there must have been 20 soldiers with machine guns pointing at our house. They knew we were Gringanistas. I remember thinking “this is not good.” Behind our house were blackberry bushes, so I took my brother and went to the neighbor’s house and I called mother to tell her not to come home. Any car coming up the hill had to either be going to the country club or to our house so I said don’t even bother. Soldiers across from La Moneda, Chile 1973 “We took off and left our house that day” You could see the planes coming by- they were fighter jets. We took off and left our house that day. You could hear the shooting, the bombings, at one point you could see the smoke of La Moneda. I slept in the living room in our friends’ house, and you could hear the guns at night outside. That really stays with you.” At the club, there were *cuidadores. I was friends with one of their daughters, and it was she who told me that they were looking for us. She told me that all the Barracloughs had to go to the police station and turn their names in. It wasn’t just us, of course. Pinochet and his command of people were going over lists of people who also needed to report in. But my friend knew where we were. So I thought, ‘wow, we’re really not very safe.’” “I had names and books in my room that could get people in trouble” Fran added, “ She was the daughter of the sergeant” and Ana continued, “Right. After that we weren’t allowed to leave the house for three days. We had a Volvo, and in Chile at the time, there weren’t that many Volvos. Also, we had diplomatic plates. So our car was very conspicuous and we didn’t dare go out in it. We wanted to put mud on the license plate and things, but after the third day I decided to just walk to our house because I had names and books in my room that could get people in trouble if the military got ahold of them. This interview was a casual conversation between Ana, her mother Fran, the director of CUSLAR, Tim, and several students and interns, including myself. There were undergraduate CUSLAR interns from both Ithaca College and Cornell, and there were also graduate students, notably international students. It was common for some of the brightest Latin American scholars at Cornell to get involved in the events and campaigns of CUSLAR. Two of these students had grown up in Argentina, another country where U.S. imperialism reared its ugly head and sought to undermine the power of popular movements. During the 40 th anniversary event, the Argentinian students asked many questions that brought our conversation to an even deeper level. One crucial piece that makes Ana’s story unique is obviously her father’s job and the specific nature of his role within the United Nations. Solon Barraclough was an American from New Hampshire who later worked with the Food and Agriculture Organization in the United Nations. After studying economics at Harvard and gaining practical knowledge on his family’s farm, Barraclough became a forester and adviser. He began working with the FAO on Latin American agriculture projects through the end of the 1950s, and, as President Kennedy launched the Alliance for Progress program in 1961. Simultaneously, a global agrarian reform movement was growing. A 2002 obituary for Solon in the Guardian stated, “Barraclough was never happier than when out in the countryside talking to peasants.” One of the Argentinian students asked Ana, if her family or her father had any diplomatic protection. She responded: “No! Even the U.N. was not protected. There were two pars to ICIRA, the national side and the U.N. side. And they found the national officials floating in Mapocho River two days after the coup. So no, there was no diplomatic protection. . . “They can’t have a coup Monday because it’s foggy” Fran: Some kid told her there was going to be a coup on Monday. And I said, “Oh the Chilean military won’t be able to do anything because it’s foggy. They can’t have a coup Monday because it’s foggy.” But it was the next day. Ana: There was no protection really for Americans. For those who were right wing, or those in the CIA, or working with the embassy, there was protection, but my father was considered a persona non grata because he was doing land reform in Chile. Chile was made up of the very wealthy and the very poor, and those who were very wealthy were the landowners who had all these *latifundios. They weren’t using the land or were planting very little, exploiting their workers. So my father was taking that land and giving it to poor farmers, dividing it up for the workers and giving them something to live on. I mean we were threatened all the time to the point where my mother said, “Move your bed away from the window.” They shot at my father’s car when he was out. When I finally left the house after the coup, I couldn’t drive our car because it was recognizable, so I walked. I remember I walked through tenement housing that was built by the Christian Democrats, built in *Educardo Frei’s time. Frei built all these bricks houses for people. “What the heck are they shooting at? This is a Christian Democrat neighborhood!” I was walking and there were helicopters flying on both sides of the road, and they were just shooting. I was thinking, “what the heck are they shooting at? This is a Christian Democrat neighborhood!” It got so that they got so close to me that I had to hide under a tree. It was spring, like that would protect me from a bullet, but that’s how naive I was, that I’m running around hiding from guns under a tree. Luckily they went away. The military broke into our house that night, on September 11. They said they were looking for weapons, but we had no weapons. They took our kitchen knives and said we had weapons. Fran: We had shish kabob sticks- real weapons! Ana: They stole all of our radios, our washing machine, anything that we had imported without paying taxes. I had books in my room with lots of names of my friends who were against the coup. I stupidly thought, “Well, I can’t put them in the fireplace because that smoke coming up the chimney will look suspicious.” So what did I do? I threw them all out the window and had a huge bonfire in the back of my house. This was about the 13th or 14th, one of the first day we could go out. So what happens? I’m standing at my house, alone, with this huge bonfire and here comes a helicopter. The helicopter shows up, maybe 50 meters above me, circling me. I’m thinking “If I run, they’ll shoot. If I go in the house, and they follow me in there, then no one is going to know.” And I’m thinking “Ahhh,” so I just stood there. I’m not really looking at them, I’m thinking “How am I going to get out of this one?” And you know, I really was saved because all they did was circle maybe 30 times, and they just yelled obscenities, because there was a blonde girl, 18 years old with hair down to her waist. I thought they might not shoot but I might get killed or raped. I have to say, I just stood there, mostly because I was kind of frozen there scared. And they left me. Photo from the Cornell Library Archives, Emergency Committee to Save Chilean Health Workers ad in The Washington Post, May 4, 1974 “It changed those people” The other thing that I did after the coup was that I went to a very good friend’s house who lived across the street from the Military Hospital. And he took me to his sister’s house near the *National Stadium. They were right-wing, some CDs, but they were horrified. They lived on Avenida Iglesia, so they were just seeing truckloads of dead bodies that were piled in the back and covered only with a tarp. My friends didn’t know what to make of it, I mean they were all for the coup, but then they started seeing these trucks at 5 or 6 o’clock in the morning. They were removing bodies from the National Stadium. It changed those people. And I kept hearing about different friends who’d been shot and detained. Fran: One called and said the soldiers came and pushed the Cardinal, who was his neighbor, into a car and took him off. Student: Some of the people who committed those crimes are now in government. They just want the people to forget. Ana: Well, you can’t forget! We have two parts of Chile, those who favored the coup and think Pinochet was a hero, and those who had family members who were disappeared or tortured or killed. They’re still finding bones. .. The Trip Out We left on the first plane that left on the 19th of September. The only reason we got out was because we had friends give us their tickets. . . (To Be Continued in Part 2) Lessons from Part 1: I haven’t talked a lot about the History is Ours project or the Chilean coup very much in recent years. I attribute that in part to my own frustration over never having brought the stories to a wider audience. I also had the time to observe over the years, that many Americans, simply did not care to know more about it. They certainly didn’t care to reflect on the U.S.’s role in this horrendous event and what it could possibly mean about U.S. foreign policy and the many, still entrenched, neoliberal institutions that hold such unbalanced power today. It’s possible that I had been so shocked and overwhelmed by the information, shocked about the coup and the things that were done to uplift fascism, shocked of course about the US’s involvement, but also shocked by the entire Western colonial project, that I went into a rather prolonged state of freeze after absorbing these stories that didn’t serve anyone, least of all the people whose stories I still held. I tried to share the stories of course in 2014 when the booklet was published. At CUSLAR, we always thought we would return to the project, revisit the interviewees, and keep telling the many unheard stories of those in Chile during this critical time period. From 2015-2018 I would bring it up at new jobs as I tried to describe who I was to co-workers; I felt like I could not relate to people my age very well without first telling them about these interviews, the book, and what had been my primary focus for that last year and my biggest accomplishment so far. The research never felt over. The layers behind this event would keep unfolding before me. I had to keep talking about it, always gauging what regular people knew about it, gauging their reactions when I told them about the coup, and gauging their reactions when they learned about the levels the U.S. was willing to go to in order to enforce its economic agenda on Chile, and anyone else that went against it. I eventually met other people interested in Chile through socialist activism in the U.S. I learned the story of my friend Alice Embree who had gone to Chile on the same trip as future Congressman Lloyd Doggett while they were both students at the University of Texas in 1967. She became a fierce antiwar activist with groups like the UT SDS chapter and the Austin Committee for Human Rights in Chile; she worked with *NACLA and, from then to today, has always spoken about Chile. Meeting Alice and her family made me feel like Chile always finds a way back into my life (more on that in Part Two). Chile has long been described as a testing ground for the *Chicago Boys Economic project. The military junta regime was a Western colonial project, similar to Israel, similar to the United States itself. The project had to succeed because socialism needed to fail; whatever would uplift the people, whatever methods that would give them their land back or give them real economic power, had to fail. Chile was to be the example. MAY 1972 General Pinochet to the left, President Allende in car, AP File Ana’s story shows that not even the UN had protection from this kind of fascist takeover. As Allende said in his final speech over the airwaves on the morning of the 11th: “At this definitive moment, the last moment when I can address you, I wish you to take advantage of the lesson: foreign capital, imperialism, together with the reaction, created the climate in which Armed Forces broke their tradition, the tradition taught by General Schneider and reaffirmed by commander Araya, victims of the same social sector which will today be in their homes hoping with foreign assistance, to retake power to continue to defend their profits and their privileges” “I am certain that the seed which we have planted in the good conscience of thousands and thousands of Chileans will not be shriveled forever. They have strength and will be able to dominate us, but social processes can be arrested neither by crime nor force. History is ours, and people make history.” Allende understood that he had been betrayed by multiple figures and elements of the military, including “Mr. Mendoza, the despicable general who only yesterday pledged his fidelity and loyalty to the Government.” Allende also understood that the military had the greater show of strength in this case. There is much debate on whether he should have done more, if he should have armed the workers, but my view, with Hindsight 20-20, after seeing the same pattern repeated successfully by the global elite in country after country; the people of Chile did not stand much of a chance against this fascist wave at that time. The people could not overpower a military leaders, many trained at the *School of the Americas, who were more brutal than any average person would have expected. The forces of foreign capital and imperialism were waging economic warfare against Chile from the moment Allende began his presidency and before. They sowed division between the classes with great intention and strategy. Ana’s experience even as part of an American elite family shows that human rights and international order would be discarded fully by the military regime and those who supported it. Does it show the weakness of the United Nations in protecting civilians? It’s unavoidable; yes. Whether it be a U.S.-backed coup in Chile, or a U.S.-sponsored genocide in Palestine, the UN seems unprepared to adequately respond and uphold international law when the violator is the United States or one of its close allies and proxies. Nixon & Kissinger, White House, October 1973, National Archive/Newsmakers via Getty Images The biggest lesson to me that needs to be remembered today is simply understanding who the United States is. These are the questions I hope someone hearing this for the first time wants to ask: Why would the United States back a coup that killed agriculture officials? Why would they back a coup that threw people doing land reform in the river? Why would they back a coup where civilians were rounded up and taken to a soccer stadium to be tortured and killed, their bodies piled onto trucks with a loose tarp and then driven to a dumping ground? If you think this started with Donald J. Trump, you have a lot to catch up on. Fascism in the United States is not new. It is not modern. Heed the last words of President Salvador Allende: “I wish you to take advantage of the lesson: foreign capital, imperialism, together with the reaction, created the climate in which Armed Forces broke their tradition.” Fascism will, and will not, creep up on you. There are signs, there are subtle ways the leaders may try to hide their fullest intentions temporarily, but a fascist’s true desire will always become apparent at a certain point, undeniably. Like the Nazi that showed up to a warehouse in Los Angeles to debate Mehdi Hasan for Jubilee , fascists will loudly proclaim their beliefs, they will laugh them off with no hesitation or second thought. Fascists, by definition, believe in power; they believe that corporate power, military power, should be the deciding factor to all government decisions. They are happy to be the axe that is wielded for that agenda. If they want to break their oaths to the Constitution, they will. You will know when fascism is at your door. And it will be far too late then. What will you do when you know when they are down the street? What will you do when you know they are a few neighborhoods over? What will you do if they go first to a neighborhood that you don’t particularly like? Will you still know that it is fascism? What will you do when you hear the stories of this coup, of what the U.S. was willing to do, of what the U.S. did , to cement its economic power over Chile, what the U.S. did to protect the international elites in the copper industry who were losing profits? Will you believe that capitalists are confident in their economic model? If in a democratic system, capitalism is always the logical choice of the people . . . why did they need the military to enforce that system? Why did they need to torture those who committed the ultimate “crime” to fascists: having their own thoughts? Believing in an alternative economic model? Joining a workers’ union, organizing as a student for a better world, supporting your neighbors, supporting land reform, speaking out against the military regime… all crimes. There comes a day when fascism is at your door, but before then, you must always organize for the power of the people, no matter who is elected, because the imperialists, the real criminals, are still at large. Allende said “ People make history.” He knew that it was the belief of the working people of Chile for a better future that put him into office in the first place. He knew that it was the power of the people (and his administration’s policies that were enacting real change for the people) that became such a threat to the global elite, they conspired to orchestrate such a violent, dissent-crushing coup. It was the threat of the people realizing their own power, through these policies, and through the broader socialist movement, that terrified them most of all. Democratic Socialism and the nationalization of the copper industry, was the threat they needed to stop before the rest of the capitalist world could truly learn the lessons of the Allende government. The U.S. would support any government who promised to squash a movement led by the coalition of leftist organizations that backed Allende’s election, and the multi-pronged workers’ movement that gave those organizations their heart and soul. The U.S. could not allow Chile’s significant improvements regarding agrarian reform, healthcare reform, worker ownership, and nationalization of industries, to become worldwide success stories. They needed the world to believe privatization and capitalism were synomynous with democracy. It was always a lie. It is still a lie. It was not socialism nor a democratic socialist government enacting land reform reforms that lead to a daughter of an American diplomat burning books to hide their friends’ names, to keep them from being targets of brutal torture and “interogation”… it was when a fascist coup occured, backed by her own government, the American government itself, that such actions were necessary. That occurs when democracy has been betrayed and U.S.-backed fascism has won. Even so, history IS ours. We, the people, make history. Democratic Socialism isn’t about a powerful leader coming to save you; it’s about the people -and only ever the people- saving themselves, no matter the time, no matter the obstacle. Foreign capital and the forces of imperialism will no longer divide us, and they will no longer defeat us. For sources and footnotes, go to the Substack article here .
